strengths: Addresses a real gap in visual-prosthesis literature: prior brain-encoding work (Granley et al., Wang et al. 2024a) does not use real brain responses as supervision, so this paper's use of paired image-brain datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG) as direct supervision is a reasonable and useful framing.
Evaluates the framework on two modalities (EEG and MEG) and across all subjects in both datasets, which is more comprehensive than many single-dataset studies.
Includes an ablation comparing cross-attention against simple addition and concatenation fusion strategies for both datasets and both metrics (Tables 5-8).

Extensive topography visualizations for every subject (training/test/generated/difference) are provided in the appendix, offering some qualitative insight into where the model succeeds or fails spatially.
weaknesses: No comparison against any existing published method (e.g., the explicitly cited 'most similar' work Lu & Golomb 2024, or GAN-based EEG generation baselines) using the same evaluation protocol/metrics — only an internal fusion-mechanism ablation is reported, so the actual advance over prior art is unverified.

Reported PCC values are very low (≈0.12–0.19 within-subject, ≈0.05–0.10 cross-subject), and the paper does not compare against a noise ceiling, random/chance baseline, or simple regression baseline (e.g., ridge regression, common in encoding-model literature) to contextualize whether these correlations reflect meaningful signal or are barely above chance.

The central claim of 'biologically plausible' brain signal generation is not actually validated: there is no downstream task (e.g., feeding generated signals through a phosphene/decoding model, or measuring whether generated signals preserve stimulus-relevant information) to demonstrate biological or functional plausibility beyond raw MSE/PCC against ground truth.

The topography visualizations (Figs. 3–8) often show generated EEG/MEG topographies that look qualitatively quite different from real/test topographies (larger amplitude spread, different polarity patterns), which undercuts rather than supports the plausibility claim, yet the text does not critically discuss these visible discrepancies.

The differences between cross-attention, addition, and concatenation in the ablation (e.g., MSE 0.217 vs 0.227 vs 0.228 on EEG) are small and not accompanied by any statistical significance testing or variance estimates across runs, making the claimed superiority of cross-attention inconclusive.

Technical novelty is limited: the method is a fairly standard application of CLIP-conditioned, cross-attention U-Net DDPMs (already widely used for image/text conditioning) to a new output modality (EEG/MEG), without new architectural or algorithmic contributions specific to the brain-signal domain.

No code/data release or detailed hyperparameter/preprocessing description sufficient for reproducibility (e.g., normalization of MSE across differently scaled EEG/MEG signals is not explained, and 'same preprocessing as Song et al. 2025' is not elaborated).

Limitations discussion is very brief (a single sentence about computational constraints) and does not address the low correlation values, lack of baselines, or the disconnect between the stated motivation (improving visual prostheses) and the lack of any prosthesis-relevant downstream evaluation.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., a first-person singular slip 'I have plotted the topography' in Section 4.4 despite the paper otherwise using 'we') suggest incomplete proofreading.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem (image-to-brain-signal generation) and provides a clear, well-documented architecture combining DiT, cross-attention with unified CLIP image+text embeddings, and a spatio-temporal position encoding scheme tailored to M/EEG channel topography.

Extensive appendices provide good reproducibility detail: full DDIM formulation, position-embedding construction (including explicit channel-to-region mappings for EEG and MEG), training/inference pseudocode, dataset preprocessing steps, and hyperparameters.

Reasonably thorough ablations (removal of text embeddings, region embeddings, temporal embeddings; comparison of three different captioning LLMs; per-brain-region channel ablation) that consistently support the design choices and align qualitatively with known visual-processing neuroscience (occipital region importance).

Within-subject results show consistent improvement over the chosen baselines across four metrics on two datasets, and the cross-subject experiments honestly expose the challenge of inter-individual variability rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch with the stated application: real visual prostheses require generating electrical stimulation parameters (amplitude, frequency, pulse width) for implanted electrode arrays, not non-invasively recorded scalp M/EEG signals. The paper never bridges this gap—there is no discussion or experiment connecting generated M/EEG signals to actual stimulus parameters or phosphene models—so the central motivating claim ("advancing visual prosthesis brain encoding") is not substantiated by the actual method or evaluation.

Baselines are weak and somewhat mismatched: Güçlü et al. (2015) and Yamins et al. (2014) are decade-old linear-regression-on-CNN-feature encoding models never designed to predict single-trial raw M/EEG waveforms, and SynBrain is an fMRI-specific VAE method adapted post hoc. No comparison to more directly relevant EEG/MEG generation approaches (e.g., GAN-based EEG synthesis mentioned in related work) or to a trivial "average ERP" baseline is provided, making the claimed superiority hard to contextualize.

The core "biological plausibility" claim is only loosely supported: metrics are MSE/Pearson/cosine/SL between single generated trials and ground truth, with no report of the inherent trial-to-trial noise ceiling of real brain data, no statistical testing/error bars, and unclear treatment of diffusion-model stochasticity (is a single sample compared, or are multiple samples averaged?). The topography figures mainly illustrate cross-subject variability rather than validating that within-subject generated signals are neurophysiologically plausible.

Use of Synchronization Likelihood as a signal-vs-signal similarity metric is non-standard (SL is typically used to measure inter-channel/inter-region synchronization, not generated-vs-real signal fidelity), and its application here is not well justified or validated against established EEG/MEG generation quality metrics.

Cross-subject generalization is very poor (e.g., MEG cross-subject Pearson drops to 0.082, EEG cross-subject Pearson drops from 0.425 to 0.157), which substantially undermines the practical significance of the approach for any real assistive application where per-patient calibration data would be scarce; this limitation is acknowledged but not mitigated or deeply analyzed.

Methodological novelty is incremental: the core contribution largely assembles known components (DiT, DDIM, CLIP cross-attention conditioning, LLM captioning, learnable positional embeddings) in a new but not conceptually novel combination; no code/data release is mentioned, limiting independent verification of the many implementation-specific choices (e.g., MVNN whitening, channel reordering/padding for region embeddings).

strengths: The paper addresses an under-explored problem (image-to-brain-signal encoding) relative to the well-studied brain decoding direction, and provides a reasonably complete architectural description (DiT+DDIM, cross-attention with CLIP image/text embeddings, learnable spatio-temporal position encodings).
Extensive appendix material (algorithms, dataset preprocessing, metric definitions) supports partial reproducibility.

Ablations for each proposed component (text embeddings, region embeddings, temporal embeddings) and for different caption-generating LLMs are provided on both datasets, showing internal consistency of design choices.
The brain-region ablation result (occipital cortex being most important) is a sensible sanity check that aligns with known visual neuroscience.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch with the stated application: actual retinal/visual prostheses stimulate ganglion cells with electrode current patterns, not by literally reproducing M/EEG waveforms; the paper never explains how a generated 'brain signal' would translate into an actual electrode stimulus for a prosthesis, so the central motivating narrative ("filling the brain-encoding gap for visual prostheses") is not technically substantiated and appears to be a re-branding of a signal-regression problem.

No noise ceiling or trial-repeatability analysis is provided. EEG/MEG single-trial responses are extremely noisy and variable even across repeated presentations of the same stimulus to the same subject; without reporting how well repeated real trials correlate with each other, it is impossible to judge whether a Pearson r of 0.38–0.43 (or MEG cross-subject r of 0.08) reflects meaningful biological plausibility or is simply within/below the noise floor.

Baselines are weak and outdated for the task: Güçlü & Van Gerven (2015) and Yamins et al. (2014) are decade-old fMRI/single-unit ventral-stream encoding papers never designed for temporal M/EEG generation, and SynBrain is an fMRI method adapted post hoc without evidence of careful re-tuning for M/EEG; no strong, modern EEG/MEG-specific generative baseline is compared.

No qualitative/quantitative validation that the generated signals are usable for any downstream purpose (e.g., feeding generated EEG into an existing decoding model and checking if decoding accuracy/reconstructed images match those from real EEG), which would be the most convincing evidence of 'biological plausibility' and of practical value for the claimed application.

Cross-subject generalization collapses dramatically (e.g., MEG cross-subject Pearson drops from 0.379 to 0.082, EEG from 0.425 to 0.157), which undermines any practical usefulness for prosthesis deployment where per-patient encoding models trained on paired brain-image data would be impractical to obtain; this critical limitation is acknowledged but not analyzed with any mitigation strategy (e.g., subject-invariant embeddings, few-shot calibration).

Methodological novelty is limited: the work largely combines existing components (DiT, DDIM, CLIP cross-attention conditioning, LLM captioning, learnable positional embeddings) in a fairly direct manner; none of the individual pieces introduces a new theoretical or algorithmic insight for the brain-signal generation problem.

The evaluation metrics (MSE, Pearson, cosine similarity, SL) are all computed against a fixed reference signal at the raw-waveform level, which is a debatable choice for the highly stochastic, non-stationary nature of M/EEG; no discussion of what constitutes a practically or clinically meaningful improvement in these metrics is offered.

The captions/ CLIP-score analysis (Section 4.3) measures caption-image alignment, not caption-brain-signal usefulness, so it does not directly justify why better captions causally improve brain-signal generation beyond a plausible narrative; the causal link is only supported indirectly via the ablation table.

Figures 3 and 7 illustrating cross-subject topography differences are descriptive but do not quantify the source of variability or suggest how the framework could be adapted to handle it, limiting their scientific contribution beyond confirming a well-known challenge in M/EEG research.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem (image-to-M/EEG 'brain encoding') that has received far less attention than brain decoding, and situates it clearly within the visual-prosthesis pipeline narrative in the introduction.

The engineering pipeline is reasonably well described and reproducible: architecture details, hyperparameters, preprocessing steps, and training/inference algorithms are all provided in the appendix, which aids replication.

Reasonably thorough ablations (CLIP text embeddings, brain-region embeddings, temporal embeddings, brain-region removal, LLM choice) that generally support the design choices and produce a neuroscientifically sensible finding (occipital cortex contributes most, consistent with its role in early visual processing).
Evaluation spans two modalities (EEG and MEG) and both within-subject and cross-subject settings, with an honest report of the cross-subject generalization gap rather than hiding it.
Multiple quantitative metrics (MSE, Pearson, Cosine, SL) are used, including a nonlinear synchronization measure that is arguably more relevant to brain-signal fidelity than simple correlation.
weaknesses: Conceptual mismatch with the stated application: visual prostheses require converting images into stimulation parameters for an implanted electrode array (as shown in the paper's own Figure 1), not into scalp-level M/EEG signals. The paper never closes the loop by showing how a generated M/EEG signal could be translated into electrode stimuli or evaluated for phosphene/visual-perception quality, so the central motivating claim (advancing the 'brain encoding' stage of visual prostheses) is largely unsubstantiated by the experiments actually performed.

Methodological novelty is modest: the approach largely assembles existing off-the-shelf components (DiT, DDIM, CLIP, LLM captioning, standard cross-attention) applied to a new signal domain; the main new element (additive learnable region+temporal position embeddings) is a fairly simple design that is not deeply analyzed beyond ablation.

Baselines are weak and dated: Güçlü et al. (2015) and Yamins et al. (2014) are decade-old linear-regression-on-CNN-feature encoding models, not modern competitors. SynBrain is an fMRI-specific method adapted with insufficient detail on how it was reimplemented/tuned for M/EEG, raising concerns about whether the comparison is fair or merely reflects a poorly adapted baseline. No comparison to modern EEG/MEG generative methods (e.g., GAN-based EEG generators cited in Section 2.3) is provided despite being directly relevant.

Cross-subject performance collapses (e.g., MEG Pearson drops from 0.379 to 0.082), essentially indicating the model does not generalize across individuals; this is acknowledged but not meaningfully addressed, undermining claims of practical usefulness for a device intended for diverse patients.

No statistical significance testing, variance/error bars, or confidence intervals are reported for the main results, ablations, or LLM-caption comparisons, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust.

The LLM caption-quality analysis (Section 4.3) is somewhat superficial: it mainly shows a larger/more recent VLM (Qwen2-VL) yields higher CLIP-score captions than smaller/older baselines, an expected and not particularly informative result, and does not probe why or how caption quality causally improves brain-signal generation beyond an ablation table.

'Biological plausibility' claims are supported only by correlation-type metrics against heavily averaged/denoised test signals (e.g., 80 repetitions per EEG test image), without comparison to a noise ceiling or human inter-trial reliability, which weakens the strength of this central claim.
